briefs.headline: Bengals hold Chase and Higgins out of Wednesday practice
briefs.summary: Cincinnati's first Week 5 injury report Wednesday listed Ja'Marr Chase (concussion) and Tee Higgins (groin, neck) as did-not-participate, with safeties Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger also out of practice; B.J. Hill was a full participant.

briefs.headline: Iraola has Isak and Gakpo in doubt for Liverpool v Man City
briefs.summary: Liverpool coach Andoni Iraola said Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo "are both injured" after leaving the Sweden and Netherlands camps, and it is a question of whether they recover for Sunday's 11:30 a.m. ET match with Manchester City.

briefs.headline: Browns' Gabriel practices in full; Graham sits out Wednesday
briefs.summary: Cleveland's Week 5 report lists QB Dillon Gabriel (back) and C Elgton Jenkins (concussion) as full participants Wednesday, while DT Mason Graham (knee, ankle), G Teven Jenkins and DE Derek Barnett sat out before Sunday at the Jets.

briefs.headline: Gibson says Marshall 'can't tackle' ahead of Coastal visit
briefs.summary: Marshall coach Tony Gibson said "we can't tackle" after Saturday's loss at James Madison; the Herd rank 129th of 138 FBS teams in 10-plus-yard plays allowed before Saturday's 7 p.m. ET game against Coastal Carolina.

briefs.headline: Tottenham's Tel equals France U21 scoring record
briefs.summary: Mathys Tel's hat trick for France Under-21s against Switzerland Tuesday took him to 17 goals, level with Odsonne Edouard's record; bottom-placed Tottenham go to Manchester United Saturday with Porro and van Hecke doubts.

briefs.headline: Road teams sweep a four-game playoff day as three series end
briefs.summary: The Dodgers, Brewers and Rays all clinched on the road Wednesday, the first four-game playoff day won entirely by visitors, and Cleveland forced an ALDS Game 4. NLCS Game 1 is Sunday in Milwaukee, ALCS Game 1 Monday in St. Petersburg.

briefs.headline: Pages' two-run single sends Dodgers past Braves 4-1 into NLCS
briefs.summary: Andy Pages, hitless through the first two games, singled home two runs in the seventh Wednesday as Los Angeles closed out Atlanta 3-1 in the NLDS. The Dodgers face Milwaukee in a rematch starting Sunday.

briefs.headline: Rays sweep Yankees with 4-3 win after fan interference call
briefs.summary: Victor Mesa Jr.'s two-run homer in the sixth held up Wednesday after Anthony Volpe's apparent tying homer was ruled a double on fan interference. Tampa Bay's first best-of-five sweep sends it to the ALCS, opening Monday at home.

briefs.headline: Ravens trade for Eagles center Cam Jurgens a day after Johnson retires
briefs.summary: Baltimore sent a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-rounder to Philadelphia on Wednesday for the two-time Pro Bowl center and a 2027 seventh. The Ravens had lost three centers to injured reserve; Jurgens is in concussion protocol.

briefs.headline: Capitals beat Penguins 5-3 in Ovechkin's last home opener
briefs.summary: Tom Wilson had a goal and two assists and Anthony Beauvillier scored 23 seconds in as Washington won Wednesday in the final home opener of Alex Ovechkin's career. Bryan Rust scored in his season debut for Pittsburgh.

briefs.headline: Oilers score five in second period to beat Ducks 5-2
briefs.summary: Evan Bouchard had two goals and an assist, Leon Draisaitl four assists and Connor McDavid three points as Edmonton erased a 2-0 deficit Wednesday in Anaheim. The Oilers are 3-0-1 to start the season.

briefs.headline: NFL and union agree drinking celebrations are no longer fouls
briefs.summary: A joint statement Wednesday said gestures imitating drinking a beverage will not draw discipline, after 20 celebration fines in Weeks 2 and 3. Fines for Kyle Juszczyk and Jake Ferguson were rescinded on appeal.

briefs.headline: Arteta signs Arsenal contract running to 2030
briefs.summary: Arsenal said Wednesday that Mikel Arteta, 44, has extended a deal that was due to expire this season. He won the club's first league title in 22 years last season and reached the Champions League final.

briefs.headline: Kyushu tournament sign goes up in Fukuoka; tickets already gone
briefs.summary: The gomen-fuda, the wooden sign announcing a basho (tournament), went up Thursday at Fukuoka Kokusai Center for the Kyushu meet, which runs Nov. 8 to 22. Advance tickets sold out on presale's first day for a second straight year, Kyodo reported.

briefs.headline: Fujinokawa resumes sparring on autumn tour ahead of Kyushu
briefs.summary: Sekiwake (third-highest rank) Fujinokawa, 21, who beat all three ozeki (champion rank) in September, won three of six bouts Thursday at the jungyo (regional tour) stop in Sayama, his first sparring since the basho (tournament), Sanspo wrote.

The reference calendar lists October as the peak of the spot run. Tarpon are unlawful to possess.

sections.label: On the Water
sections.note: All four waters reported from the locked fishing.json, generated_at 2026-10-08T05:43:27-04:00, errors list empty; the file was not re-run by this desk and every figure is printed as it stands there. The fetcher's '24h ago' comparison points on all three USGS gauges are again the first point of its two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday, not the true 24-hour mark: Williams 83.8 cfs and 1.54 feet against a true mark of 71.4 and 1.46 at 5:15 a.m. Wednesday, Point Pleasant 24.5 against 24.44 at 5 a.m. Wednesday, Huntington 25.82 against 26.17 at 5 a.m. Wednesday (each true mark is Wednesday's edition reading). Williams: falling flag right on the day, down 8.6 cfs and 0.06 feet in an unbroken recession, and right at the hour by one gauge step (64.2 at 4 a.m. to 62.8 at 5:15, with a 64.2 flicker at 4:45), though the fetcher's 21.0-cfs drop is two and a half times the true one; prime wading water for a tenth morning, the window's low. Point Pleasant: rising flag right on the day, up 0.36 from Wednesday's 24.44, and wrong at the hour, the pool having peaked at 24.97-24.98 between 3 and 3:30 a.m. and shed 0.18 since. Huntington: steady flag wrong on the day, down 0.32 from Wednesday's 26.17, and wrong at the hour, up 0.23 since 3 a.m. and 0.12 in the last hour inside the usual chop. The Summersville release stepped down once more on the USGS trace: 03189600 below the dam fell from 9.44 feet at 5 a.m. Wednesday to 7.73 by 9 a.m. and has held 7.73-7.75 for 20 hours to 4:45 a.m.; the Gauley above Belva (03192000) ran Wednesday's overnight pulse through, 517 cfs at 6 a.m. up to 1,400 at noon and back down to 479 cfs and 1.86 feet from 3 to 5 a.m. today, the window's low and flat; 03189100 is the Gauley near Craigsville, above the lake, 250 cfs and 10.61 feet at 5:30 a.m. against 288 Wednesday. Those are readings of the USGS traces pulled at 5:51 a.m., not Corps statements; the Corps' Huntington District site was not opened today because Wednesday's open served only a JavaScript shell, so no lake level is printed. NWS at 5:51 a.m.: no product active anywhere in West Virginia; nothing for Coastal Pender (NCZ106) or Coastal New Hanover (NCZ108), so the Topsail block carries no beach-weather line. USNO phases API answered this morning: new moon Saturday, Oct. 10, 15:50 UT, re-verified.

waters.reading: 62.8 cfs, 1.4 feet at 5:15 a.m., flagged falling against 83.8 cfs and 1.54 feet in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.working: Ten mornings of prime wading water and the slowest recession yet. The USGS two-day trace, pulled at 5:51 a.m., runs the river down a step a few hours with no rise in it: 71.4 cfs and 1.46 feet at 5:15 a.m. Wednesday, the true 24-hour mark and Wednesday's edition reading, 71.4 through 8:45 a.m., 69.9 from 9 a.m. through 1:45 p.m., 68.5 from 2 through 4 p.m., 67.0 from 4:15 through 8 p.m., 65.6 from 8:15 p.m. through 1:45 a.m., 64.2 from 2 through 4 a.m., then 62.8 at 4:15 and 4:30, a 64.2 flicker at 4:45, and 62.8 cfs and 1.40 feet at 5 and 5:15 a.m., the window's low. Against the true 24-hour mark that is down 8.6 cfs and 0.06 feet on the day, a third less than Wednesday's 12.4-cfs drop, so the fetcher's falling flag is right on the day and right at the hour by a single gauge step, the river now moving between two adjacent readings. Its 83.8 cfs and 1.54 feet comparison point is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday (this morning's pull starts at 6 a.m. Tuesday at 83.8 and 1.54, and Wednesday's edition recorded the same pair at 5:15 a.m. Tuesday), not 24 hours ago; it makes the drop look like 21.0 cfs, two and a half times the true 8.6. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, prime wading water, the lowest number of the ten-day run. The Weather Service's active list for West Virginia carried no product at 5:51 a.m., no frost advisory for Pocahontas, where the river rises, and no fog statement. At 63 cfs, ten days into a recession that has slowed to a step every few hours, this is as thin and clear as the river has been this fall, and the pocket water fishes like a spring creek: a 12-foot leader to 6X or 7X, a size 18 or 20 Blue-Winged Olive or Parachute Adams over the tailouts once the sun is on the water and the olives start, a size 18 Pheasant Tail or Zebra Midge on a short dropper under the dry through the plunge-pool heads, where the fish hold in the only depth left, a size 16 soft hackle swung through the tailouts midday, and a size 12 or 14 October Caddis dry alone over the undercut banks in the last hour of light, the one big bite on the river; with the stonefly nymphs under the rocks rather than on the water in October, a small black stonefly nymph on the dropper is the other choice through the plunge pools. Approach from downstream, stay on the gravel, and make the first cast count, because at this flow every fish in a pool sees the wade; a small olive sculpin stripped tight to the undercuts is a last-light bet only on water this thin. WVDNR's fall trout guide page, opened again this morning and still last modified Sept. 15, says select streams and lakes will be stocked with catchable-size trout the weeks of Oct. 19 and Oct. 26, more than 40,000 pounds in about 40 waters, most of them one to two pounds, and names the Cranberry and the Elk among its picks; the Williams is not named on that page.
waters.note: The fetcher's 83.8 cfs and 1.54 feet comparison point is the first point of its two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday, not 24 hours ago; this morning's USGS pull (period P2D at 5:51 a.m.) begins at 6 a.m. Tuesday at 83.8 and 1.54, and Wednesday's edition recorded 83.8 and 1.54 at 5:15 a.m. Tuesday. The trace's true 24-hour mark is 71.4 cfs and 1.46 feet at 5:15 a.m. Wednesday, Wednesday's edition reading, so the river is down 8.6 cfs and 0.06 feet on the day and the falling flag is right on the day and right at the hour (64.2 from 2 to 4 a.m., 62.8 at 4:15 and 4:30, 64.2 at 4:45, 62.8 at 5 and 5:15). The fetcher's numbers, flag and read string are printed as written; the Dyer gauge's latest point is 5:15 a.m. No water temperature was pulled this morning (the Dyer gauge reports none and the Craigsville thermometer was not requested), so none is printed. The Weather Service's active list for West Virginia (api.weather.gov/alerts/active?area=WV), opened 5:51 a.m., returned zero features. The trout guide page (wvdnr.gov/fall-trout-fishing-guide/) answered HTTP 200 with Last-Modified Tue, 15 Sep 2026 16:16:53 GMT and article:modified_time 2026-09-15T20:16:53+00:00, unchanged from Wednesday; its text names the Cranberry River and the Elk River among fall picks and does not contain the word Williams. 'Spring creek' is a comparison of how it fishes, not a classification; 'clear' is not gauged, and the trace shows no rise in ten days. The stonefly line is grounded in the water's listed forage, not a hatch report.

waters.working: Up a third of a foot on the day, but the pool topped out at 3 a.m. and is already easing off it. The trace, pulled at 5:51 a.m., runs 24.44 at 5 a.m. Wednesday, the true 24-hour mark and Wednesday's edition reading, 24.35 at 5:45, 24.43 at 6, the window's low of 24.34 at 11:15 a.m., 24.47 at noon, 24.51 at 3 p.m., 24.62 at 6, 24.74 at 9, 24.97 at midnight, 24.95 at 2:45 a.m., 24.97 at 3, 24.98 at 3:30, the overnight high, 24.85 at 3:45, 24.80 at 4, 24.83 at 4:15, 24.81 at 4:30, 24.79 at 4:45 and 24.80 at 5 a.m. That is up 0.36 on the day, so the fetcher's rising flag is right on the day, and down 0.18 from the 3:30 a.m. high, flat to a hundredth over the last hour, so the flag is wrong at the hour, where the pool is easing or steady. Its 24.5 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday (this morning's pull begins at 6 a.m. Tuesday at 24.51), not 24 hours ago; this time it happens to sit close to the true mark, so the rise it implies, 0.3, is about the true 0.36. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, normal pool, ordinary bank access. Upstream the Summersville release stepped down once more on the USGS trace: 03189600 below the dam, stage only, read 9.44 feet at 5 a.m. Wednesday, 9.08 at 5:15, 8.93 at 6, 7.73 by 9 a.m., and has held 7.73 to 7.75 for 20 hours through 4:45 a.m. today; the Gauley above Belva, USGS 03192000, carried Wednesday's overnight pulse through, 537 cfs at 5 a.m. Wednesday, 517 at 6, 919 at 9, 1,400 at noon, 1,250 at 3 p.m., 903 at 6, 653 at 9, 517 at midnight and 479 cfs and 1.86 feet from 3 through 5 a.m. today, the window's low and flat for two hours, a sixth of the 2,700 cfs it carried Monday. The Gauley near Craigsville, above the lake, read 250 cfs and 10.61 feet at 5:30 a.m. against 288 a day earlier, the inflow still easing. The Corps' Huntington District site served only a JavaScript shell Wednesday and was not opened today, so no lake elevation and no Corps release figure is printed; the cut is a reading of the USGS traces, not a Corps statement. At 24.8, a third of a foot more water than Wednesday morning and with the Gauley share of the Kanawha down to a trickle of Monday's, the pool is high in its band and sitting still: shad are the forage and skipjack are with them, so a white or pearl swimbait or a three-quarter-ounce spoon worked across the wing dams, the fish on the downstream face and in the slack behind them with the current slackening, a half-ounce blade bait or a three-inch paddletail on a half-ounce head along the riprap at first light, a crawfish-pattern jig crawled down the riprap where it meets the mud for the smallmouth and the drum once the sun is up, and the lock wall at Byrd as the deep edge for the sauger and the hybrids on a jigging spoon or a live skipjack; with the pool flat at the hour and the extra water from Wednesday's pulse still in it, the barge cuts and the outside bends hold the catfish on cut skipjack through the morning, and the wing-dam faces get the first pass when the pool starts to drop again.

waters.near: below R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam
waters.reading: 25.85 feet at 5 a.m., flagged steady against 25.82 in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.read: 25.9 ft — normal pool. Ordinary bank access.
waters.working: Down a third of a foot on the day and climbing again at the hour, and the steady flag is wrong both ways. The trace, pulled at 5:51 a.m., runs 26.17 at 5 a.m. Wednesday, the true 24-hour mark and Wednesday's edition reading, 26.15 at 6, 26.21 at 6:30, the window's high, 26.03 at 9, 25.90 at noon, 25.87 at 3 p.m., 25.82 at 6, 25.80 at 9, 25.55 at 10 p.m., the window's low, 25.63 at midnight, 25.62 at 3 a.m., 25.74 at 3:15, 25.67 at 3:30, 25.69 at 3:45, 25.73 at 4 and 4:15, 25.80 at 4:30, 25.81 at 4:45 and 25.85 at 5 a.m. That is down 0.32 on the day, the whole of it between 6:30 a.m. and 10 p.m. Wednesday, and up 0.23 since 3 a.m. and 0.12 in the last hour inside a chop of one to two tenths quarter hour to quarter hour, so the fetcher's steady flag is wrong on the day and wrong at the hour, where the river is rising. Its 25.82 is the first point of its own two-day window, about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday (this morning's pull starts at 6 a.m. Tuesday at 25.72), not 24 hours ago; it sits three hundredths under today's number only because Tuesday morning was near the bottom of the window. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, normal pool, ordinary bank access. The Point Pleasant pool above climbed a half foot from 11:15 a.m. Wednesday to 3:30 a.m. today and has started to ease; the rise here since 3 a.m. reads like the front of that water passing the dam, about eight to 10 hours behind the pool's turn upward, and the Gauley release above was cut again Wednesday morning and the Belva gauge is at the window's low (see Point Pleasant), a reading of the USGS traces, not a Corps statement; the quarter-hour chop reads like lockages. At 25.9 with the river coming back up after a day of draining, the current below the dam is pulse current, and the fish will be on the eddy seams while a pulse runs and tucked into the rock when it slacks: the forage is shad and skipjack with crawfish in the riprap, so a white swimbait or a three-quarter-ounce spoon swum along the downstream face of the wing dams and through the eddy seam below each one when water comes through, a half-ounce blade bait along the riprap for the sauger and the smallmouth in the low light, a crawfish-colored tube or jig on the riprap toe as the sun gets up, and cut skipjack on the bottom in the barge cuts and the outside bends for the blues and the flatheads after dark; the lock wall fishes from the downstream side on a live skipjack for the hybrids when the gates open, and with the pool above turning down and this gauge turning up, the morning should carry more of that than Wednesday's did.
waters.note: This is the gauge below R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam, not the tailwater. No Weather Service product is active for Cabell or Wayne counties or anywhere in West Virginia.

waters.reading: Sound at Hampstead: low 1:01 AM at 0.5 ft, high 6:50 AM at 4.1 ft, low 1:17 PM at 0.5 ft, high 7:16 PM at 4.2 ft. Surf at Ocean City Beach pier: low 11:58 PM (Wed) at 0.3 ft, high 6:11 AM at 5.0 ft, low 12:19 PM at 0.2 ft, high 6:34 PM at 5.1 ft. Water 73.4F at Beaufort, 60 miles up the coast, observed 5:36 a.m. Moon waning crescent, 10% lit, 26.6 days old.
waters.read: Fish the moving water either side of high at 6:50 AM and 7:16 PM in the sound.
waters.working: Two days short of the new moon, 26.6 days old and 10 percent lit, the moon is a sliver and the springs are nearly here: the U.S. Naval Observatory's phase table, which answered again this morning, puts the new moon Saturday, Oct. 10, at 15:50 UT, 11:50 a.m. ET, with the first quarter Oct. 18 and the full moon Oct. 26, so the swings grow through the weekend and the inlet current with them. The sound at Hampstead came off a 0.5-foot low at 1:01 a.m. and fills 3.6 feet to a 4.1-foot high at 6:50 a.m., slack high a little after first light; it then drains the same 3.6 feet to a 0.5-foot low at 1:17 p.m., so the last two hours of the morning ebb, about 11:15 a.m. to 1:17, land in full daylight, and fills 3.7 feet in six hours to the day's big water, a 4.2-foot high at 7:16 p.m., about dusk, with the evening ebb running on into the night; all four sound events fall inside Thursday. The surf at Ocean City Beach pier runs ahead, and its first event belongs to Wednesday: low 11:58 p.m. Wednesday at 0.3, high 6:11 a.m. at 5.0, low 12:19 p.m. at 0.2, high 6:34 p.m. at 5.1; today's lags from the two tables are 39 and 42 minutes on the highs and 63 and 58 minutes on the lows, the lows again lagging longer, the long-ebb pattern. For the crew's water two miles north of the inlet, tide stage first: the red drum window is the bottom of the morning ebb, roughly 11:15 a.m. to 1:17 p.m., in daylight, and again on the evening ebb after 7:16 p.m. in the dark; the flood from 1:17 to 7:16 covers the oyster bars and grass edges and puts the drum in the flooded grass and under the docks around the 7:16 p.m. high, the highest water of the day and the last of the light; slack at 6:50 a.m., 1:17 p.m. and 7:16 p.m. is dead water. The water at Beaufort, 60 miles up the coast, read 73.4 degrees at 5:36 a.m., the same figure as Wednesday's 5:36 a.m. reading, so the three-morning slide from Sunday's 79.5 has paused for a day. What is running is a week old, not a month: the Fisherman's Post Topsail and Sneads Ferry October report posted Thursday, Oct. 1, at 9 a.m. ET, seven days ago, and the feed carried it as its newest item at 5:51 this morning. East Coast Sports has slot red drum with over-slots mixed in off the surf and piers, Spanish and bluefish plentiful, kings starting to show at the piers, and inshore red drum as the main target, scattered through the ICW, the creeks and the inlets, with no real word on trout; Native Son has mullet everywhere and reds at the docks, creek mouths and grass lines, a few trout on early topwater, glass minnows thick off the beach; Spring Tide has the reds schooled in the bays at 22 to 28 inches and better, topwater some days and cut bait others, trout quiet until it cools, and Spanish pushing inside the inlet on a high tide; Speckled Specialist has reds on Carolina-rigged live mullet, trout in the first hour of light on a Spook Jr. then live shrimp under slip corks in 15 to 20 feet, and 3- to 4-pound black drum on the bridges and oyster reefs with shrimp; Carolina Flats has big mullet in the ICW, reds on live finger mullet or Gulp under popping corks and flounder as bycatch; Plan 9 has 14- to 22-inch Spanish and false albacore in 15 to 20 feet just outside the inlet on small metal and epoxy jigs; South End Adventures has the bigger Spanish over hard bottom in 45 to 50 feet under the birds. Off the piers, Jolly Roger reports kings to 32 pounds on the bait, Spanish getting bigger, and night bottom fishing for red drum to 31 inches, Virginia mullet, pompano, bluefish, black drum and some flounder; Surf City reports good-sized Spanish on Gotcha plugs, slot and occasional over-slot reds, and evening mixed bags of black drum, mullet, spots and croakers; Seaview reports the mullet migration starting, Spanish and blues on Gotchas or diamond jigs, and flounder, sea mullet, spot, sheepshead, trout and black drum on the bottom. Coastal Angler's Topsail column is still Sept. 1, 37 days old. Setups grounded in that and today's tide: first light comes on the last of the flood toward the 6:50 a.m. slack high, so a Spook Jr. or another walking topwater over the flooded grass edges and the dock shadows for the trout in the first hour, and keep it going as the ebb gets started; as the ebb runs out toward 1:17, and especially from 11:15 on, cut mullet or a live finger mullet on a Carolina rig fan-cast a couple of feet off the creek-mouth channel edges for the drum, and a live shrimp under a slip cork in the deeper ICWW channel for the trout; on the six-hour flood from 1:17 to 7:16, a Carolina-rigged live finger mullet, the bait the whole report is built on, along the grass edges and across the oyster bars as they cover, or a Gulp shrimp or a three-inch paddletail under a popping cork drifted along the edges, and a Gotcha plug or small metal jig inside the inlet if the Spanish come in on the high as Spring Tide describes; at the 7:16 p.m. high, the day's highest water and the last of the light, a weedless gold spoon or a soft plastic on a weighted swimbait hook in the flooded grass and under the docks; on the evening ebb after dark, Carolina-rigged cut mullet again off the channel edges for the drum, and a half-ounce bucktail with a Gulp trailer bounced through the channel edges for the flounder, which are release only under proclamation FF-27-2026; and at the dock lights, with a 10 percent moon giving them almost no competition, a small white paddletail or a live shrimp under a float for the trout, with a fiddler crab or a piece of shrimp tight to the bridge pilings and oyster rocks on the moving water for the black drum and sheepshead. On the beach, the Spanish on the flooding surf from the 12:19 p.m. low toward the 6:34 p.m. high take Gotcha plugs and small metal or epoxy jigs under the birds, with the glass minnows the shops describe as the forage and false albacore mixed in outside the inlet. The reference calendar lists October as the spot run's peak, with red drum, trout, bluefish, sea mullet and black drum, and the piers' spot and croaker lines fit it.
